sentences.text: By way of filing the present revision petition, the petitioner- accused has challenged the judgment dated 04.02.2005 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge No.2, Sri Ganganagar in Criminal Appeal No. 17/2002 whereby the judgment and order of conviction dated 20.07.2002 passed by the learned Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Suratgarh, District Sri Ganganagar has been affirmed.

entities.text: Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Suratgarh, District Sri Ganganagar
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: 2. As per the prosecution, on 27.06.1997, the food inspector collected milk samples from the petitioner who is a milk vendor.
The same were sent for analysis to the Public Analyst, Sri Ganganagar alongwith one copy of Form No.7, after duly following the procedure provided under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

The public Analyst, Sri Ganganagar in its report has found the milk samples so taken to be 'Adulterated'.
[2024:RJ-JD:46341] (2 of 5) [CRLR-94/2005]
3.
On the basis of the report of the Public Analyst, the petitioner was prosecuted for the offence punishable under sections 7/16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

During the course Indraj vs State (2024:Rj-Jd:46341) on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105949857/
1 of trial the prosecution examined as many as 04 witnesses and got exhibited as many as 21 documents in the support of its case.
The prosecution further got the statements of the petitioner recorded under Section 313 of Cr.P.C.

After considering all the relevant facts and circumstances as surfacing from the face of record, the learned trial Court convicted the petitioner- accused for the aforementioned offence and sentenced him to undergo one year's simple imprisonment and fine a Rs.1000/- and in default of payment of fine to further undergo 2 months' simple imprisonment.
4. Learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that the petitioner does not have any criminal antecedents.

He further submitted that the incident in the present case occurred in the year 1997 and that there is no positive evidence available on record of the case indicating that the milk from which the samples were procured by the food inspector was willfully and intentionally adulterated by none but the petitioner himself and in the absence thereof, only on the basis of the report of Public Analyst, it cannot be said that the petitioner had committed the alleged crime or the milk was adulterated.
5.

Learned counsel further submitted that there is clear violation of Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 wherein it is mandatory to forward a copy of the report of the result of the analysis to such person or persons, as the case may be, informing such person or persons that if it is so desired, [2024:RJ-JD:46341] (3 of 5) [CRLR-94/2005] either or both of them may make an application to the Court within a period of ten days from the date of receipt of the copy of the report to get the samples of the articles of food kept by the Local (Health) Authority, analyzed by the Central Food Laboratory.

6. Lastly, learned counsel for the petitioner in the alternative submitted that since the occurrence relates to year 1997 and the petitioner has already served some part of the sentence awarded to him,
therefore the substantive sentence awarded to the petitioner may be reduced to the period already undergone by him.

Reliance was placed on the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India rendered in the case of "Puttaswamy v. State of Karnataka": 2009 (1) WLC (SC) (Cri.) 623 and a judgment of Coordinate Bench of this Court rendered in the case of "Kamla Prasad v. State of Rajasthan": 2014 CriLJ 2582.
7.

sentences.text: On the contrary, learned public prosecutor submitted that the learned Courts below have rightly awarded the sentence against the petitioner.

There is no illegality or infirmity in the impugned judgment/order passed by the learned Trial Court and affirmed by the learned Sessions Court and therefore the same does not call for any interference by this Court in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction.
8. Heard learned counsel for the parties at length.
Perused the record of the case.

9. In the case of "TN Dhakkal v. James Basnett": (2001) 10 SCC 419, the Hon'ble Apex Court has laid down the principles as to under what circumstances the revisional jurisdiction should be exercised by the High Court.

entities.text: TN Dhakkal v. James Basnett": (2001) 10 SCC 419
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant paragraphs are extracted as under:
Indraj vs State (2024:Rj-Jd:46341) on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105949857/
2 [2024:RJ-JD:46341] (4 of 5) [CRLR-94/2005] "7. By virtue of the powers under Section 401 Cr.P.C.
the High Court has jurisdiction to examine the proceedings of inferior courts if the necessity for doing so is brought to its notice in any manner.

Under Section 397 of Code, the High Court possess general power of superintendence over actions of the courts subordinate to it and that discretionary power; when administered on the judicial side, is termed as the power of "revision."

8. While giving its reasoned judgment in Janta Dal v. H.S. Chowdhray a Division Bench of this Court speaking through Pandian, J. (as his Lordship then was) dealt with the object of revisional jurisdiction of the High Court in the following words:
(SCC p. 355, para 130).
130.

The object of the revision jurisdiction under Section 401 is to confer power upon superior criminal courts-a kind of paternal or supervisory jurisdiction in order to correct miscarriage of justice arising from misconception of law, irregularity of procedure, neglect of proper precaution or appearance harshness of treatment which has resulted, on the one hand, or on the other hand in some undeserved hardship to individuals.

The controlling power of the High Court is discretionary and it must be exercised in the interest of justice with regard to all facts and circumstances of each particular case, anxious attention being given to the said and circumstances while vary greatly from case to case.

The Bench than went on to say that: SCC p. 355, para 132)
132.
The criminal courts are clothed with inherent power to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice.

Such power through unrestricted and undefined should not be capriciously or arbitrarily exercised,
but should be exercised in appropriate cases, ex debito justitiae to do real and substantial justice for the administration of which alone the court exist.
The power possessed by the High Court under Section 482 of the Code are very wide and the very plenitude of the power requires great caution in its exercise.
Courts must be careful to see that its decision in exercise of this power is based on second principles.
9. We are in agreement with the above exposition of law.

We are of the opinion that though the High Court has revisional jurisdiction to correct miscarriage of justice, but whether or not, there is justification for the exercise of that discretionary jurisdiction would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case.

The controlling power of the High Court under Section 401 of the Code being discretionary is required to be exercised only in the interest of justice, having regard to all the facts and circumstances of each particular case and not mechanically."
10.

After due consideration of facts and circumstances of the case and keeping in mind the settled law dealing with the object of the revisional jurisdiction, this Court finds that the petitioner was [2024:RJ-JD:46341] (5 of 5) [CRLR-94/2005] a milk vendor and therefore there is no reason Indraj vs State (2024:Rj-Jd:46341) on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105949857/
3 available with it to disbelief the report of analysis of the Public Analyst, Sri Ganganagar wherein the samples drawn from the milk were found to be 'Adulterated'.

However, in the opinion of this Court since the incident relates to the year 1997 and the petitioner has suffered the agony and trauma of protracted trial for about 27 years coupled with the fact that the petitioner has spent some period in custody, it will be just and proper if the sentence awarded to the petitioner by the learned Trial Court for the offence under sections 7/16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 is reduced to the period already undergone by him while directing him to deposit the fine amount, if not so already deposited.
11. In the result, the revision petition is partly allowed.

While maintaining the petitioner's conviction, the sentence awarded to him for the offence under section 7/16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 is hereby reduced to the period already undergone by him.
However, the petitioner is directed to deposit the fine amount, if not already deposited by him within a period of 2 months from the date of this order.

In default of such deposit within the stipulated period of time,
the revision petition shall stand dismissed and the petitioner shall be liable to serve the remaining sentence.
12. The record of the trial Court as well as appellate Court be sent back forthwith.
13. No order as to costs.

(KULDEEP MATHUR),J 10-himanshu/-
